blocks.heading: The darkest hour before the redemption

paragraphs.text: Speaking at a gathering for hachnasas kallah, the Rav recalls how Pharaoh suddenly stopped supplying straw yet demanded the same quota of bricks, and beat the Jews when they fell short. The hardest part of the exile, he notes, came right before the Exodus.

The same happened in the time of Mordechai and Esther. The Jews expected redemption at the end of seventy years, it did not come, and instead Haman's decree to destroy them arrived. Yet seventy days later came the miracle. These, the Rav says, were history-making days.

blocks.heading: Iran, the economy, and a hard question

paragraphs.text: In his own day, the Rav says, the world is in fear of Iran, whose leader threatens to destroy the Jews; he is a second Haman. But Iran was once Paras, where Haman fell, and a place where Jews had a miracle. The Rav hopes for a repeat of that miracle in our days.

Meanwhile parnassa is hard, people despair, and almost every week someone stands up in shul to plead for help. Hashem runs the world with hashgacha pratis, so the Rav asks: if He wants us to support others and marry off our children, why does He not give the money? It is the same decree as Pharaoh's.

To answer, the Rav turns to Yehuda and Tamar. When Tamar was found to be expecting and sentenced to be burned, she sent Yehuda his items, and he immediately declared, 'She is more righteous than I.' For Yehuda, known as the upright leader of Yaakov's family, this public shame was great mesiras nefesh, and for it Yaakov later blessed him that his brothers would praise him.

Unlike the author of Unesaneh Tokef, who asked the king for three days, Yehuda had no time: the Midrash explains that the fire had already been lit. The Rav then asks why Tamar did not openly reveal that Mashiach would come from her.

blocks.heading: The one weapon against the Satan

paragraphs.text: The Rav answers that the Satan fights hardest against Mashiach, since he will be destroyed when Mashiach comes. He caused Er and Onan to sin and die, and would have spoiled things with Yehuda too. The one weapon he cannot withstand is mesiras nefesh, so Tamar arranged that both she and Yehuda would have it.

Likewise, Lot was saved from Sodom because Hashem sent him a gift: guests. In Sodom, taking in a guest was punished; the Midrash tells that Lot's daughter was killed for giving bread to a poor man. Lot's hospitality was therefore mesiras nefesh, and in its merit he was saved.

blocks.heading: Hashem's present: tzedakah with mesiras nefesh

paragraphs.text: Mashiach must come now, the Rav says, but the Satan holds him back. So Hashem sends a present, as He did to Lot: many needy people, fathers who cannot bring a daughter to the chuppah, while the givers have only a little. Giving then takes mesiras nefesh.

He tells of Reb Aryeh in Yerushalayim, who collected door to door for each poor man, three times in three hours, explaining that the doctor prescribed a spoonful every hour. That, the Rav says, is Hashem's prescription for us.

Mesiras nefesh, the Rav explains, does not only mean being killed. Nefesh means will, as in Avraham's words to the sons of Ches, so acting against one's will for Hashem is mesiras nefesh. A woman who gives up a stylish garment that is not tzniusdig has mesiras nefesh. In these times, he says, mitzvos must be done that way.
He brings the Gemara on the verse in Malachi: reviewing a hundred times was routine, and the one who reviews the 101st time is the true oved Hashem. He closes with a brachah for the redemption.
